newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin's deals in Belarus, Chechnya face tests.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin's deals in Belarus, Chechnya face tests.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin began his first weekend out of hospital since his heart operation with two major peace deals wrapped up. But at the start of a new week his gradual return to politics looked considerably less rosy.

The political compromise he pushed for between the head of state and parliament in neighbouring Belarus lay in ruins after President Alexander Lukashenko went ahead on Sunday with a controversial referendum seeking greatly expanded powers.

And elsewhere on the troubled fringes of the former Soviet empire, Yeltsin's dramatic concession to Chechen separatist rebels, ordering the last Russian troops to leave the region, raised howls of protest from Moscow's parliamentary opposition.

"The events of the last few days, the sharp deterioration of the situation in Belarus, a string of terrorist actions in the North Caucasus and the deepening economic crisis demonstrate the incompetence of the executive," said communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, who was runner-up to Yeltsin in July's election.

At the insistence of the communists, who dominate the State Duma, the lower house summoned an emergency debate on the deal for next Friday. Zyuganov called it "unconstitutional" and a "malignant cancer" that would spread until Russia was torn apart in the way the Soviet Union was broken up in 1991.
The Duma has little power to overturn government policy, but it could, for example, make trouble for the 1997 budget, which is already in the middle of a stormy passage through parliament.
The next week in Belarus, which has the closest ties to Moscow of any former Soviet state, is also extremely unclear.

Yeltsin had created a two-state union with Lukashenko in April as a foil to Zyuganov's championing of re-integrating the former Soviet territories. But Lukashenko has irritated Russia with his slowness to allow free market democratic reforms.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who spent a sleepless night in Minsk reconciling Lukashenko and Belarus legislators on Friday, blamed a group of deputies for sabotaging the deal.
But he also criticised Lukashenko for a lack of effort.

Russia's ORT state television quoted a government spokesman denying reports Lukashenko had spoken again with Chernomyrdin. "Once again the Belarussian side is trying to use Russia's authority for its own ends. It's a pity." the spokesman said.

Yeltsin's order to withdraw the last two brigades of Russian troops from Chechnya opened the way for Chernomyrdin to sign a framework agreement with Chechen government leader Aslan Maskhadov on Saturday that lays down relations between Moscow and Grozny in the run up to Chechen elections on January 27.

In doing so, Yeltsin, who will convalesce for another fortnight or so near Moscow, has given the separatists virtually everything they had fought for since he sent the Russian army against their self-declared independent republic two years ago.

Maskhadov makes no secret of the fact that the one great outstanding issue -- that of outright secession under international law -- has merely been postponed for up to five years until Moscow can swallow even that bitter pill.
"I am saying straight out that what I want is sovereignty," Maskhadov, who masterminded the Chechens' military victory, said in an otherwise conciliatory interview on NTV television.
"That is what I fought for," he added. "I want international guarantees of the security of my people."
Liberals hailed the accord as "a victory for common sense" and accused the communists of being "the party of war".

But the communists have allies. Ultranationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky, who commands the third biggest bloc in the Duma after the communists and the government party, told NTV: "It is monstrous. It is the beginning of the break-up of Russia."

"First goes Chechnya, then other North Caucasus republics, then the Volga republics, then the Siberian ones," he said. "And then with some nice title they'll create us a Russian republic from Voronezh to Arkhangelsk (southwest and northwest Russia)."

The anchorman for NTV news commented: "It is not clear what Zyuganov is suggesting -- to go on with the war in Chechnya or something else. He did not come up with any concrete proposals of his own today on how to settle the problem."
Leading Chechen negotiator Movladi Udugov told Reuters the opposition would have rejected any deal.
